templates.title: Time to ready — minutes from a cluster request to its last node ready, per region, GPU type and week
templates.subtopic: per-entity first events, ROW_NUMBER to the n-th, percentile_cont, FILTER

sections.scenario: Customers of a GPU cloud ask for a Kubernetes-based cluster of a given size in a region and GPU type. Nodes are allocated, imaged and health-checked, and each reports ready when it can take work. The provisioning team publishes a weekly view of how long customers wait for a whole cluster, per region and GPU type, and keeps clusters that never became fully ready visible next to it rather than letting them vanish from the averages.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, region, gpu_type, ready_clusters, median_minutes, max_minutes, partial_clusters, one row per (week, region, GPU type) that has at least one request that was not cancelled, ordered by week_start, region, gpu_type. week_start is the Monday (a date) of the UTC week of requested_at. Requests with a cancelled_at are excluded entirely. A node's ready time is its first ready event. A cluster is ready at the moment its nodes_requested-th distinct node first reported ready; its time to ready is the minutes from requested_at to that moment. ready_clusters counts ready clusters; median_minutes is percentile_cont(0.5) and max_minutes the maximum of their times to ready (both NULL when no cluster in the group is ready). partial_clusters counts requests that never had nodes_requested distinct ready nodes. {{week_rule}} {{flap_rule}} {{replace_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Timestamps are whole minutes. The sample has {{requests}} requests and {{events}} node events; production has many thousands of nodes a week.
sections.assumptions: Regions, GPU types, cluster sizes and timings are hypothetical. Node states are simplified to provisioning, ready and not_ready; a real provisioning pipeline has more steps. The data was extracted after every request in it had settled.
sections.criteria: Excludes cancelled requests entirely; first ready event per node; the nodes_requested-th distinct node rather than the last; partial clusters counted apart and kept out of the median; week of the request; a row per group even when nothing in it became ready; deterministic order; sensible answers on clock start, tails and incremental maintenance.

clarifications.q: Which week does a request belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC week (Monday start) of requested_at, even if its nodes became ready the next week.

clarifications.q: A cancelled request had all its nodes ready before it was cancelled. Does it count?
clarifications.a: No. Any request with a cancelled_at is excluded from every column.

clarifications.q: A node reported ready, then not_ready, then ready again. When was it ready?
clarifications.a: At its first ready event.

clarifications.q: What if more nodes report ready than were requested?
clarifications.a: The cluster was ready when the nodes_requested-th distinct node first became ready. Later nodes do not move it.

clarifications.q: Do partial clusters count in the median?
clarifications.a: No. They have no time to ready; they appear only in partial_clusters.

hints: Reduce events first: one row per (request, node) with MIN(event_ts) over ready events.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY request_id ORDER BY first_ready) and a join on k = nodes_requested gives the moment the cluster became ready; a request with no such row is partial.
LEFT JOIN the ready times onto the non-cancelled requests, then aggregate with percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …) and COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE … IS NULL).
followups: Customers see "ready" on a status page. Should their clock start at the request, at quota approval, or at capacity being found? How would you report each without double counting?
Some clusters sit partial for days. Add a column for the age of the oldest partial cluster per group, and say what the query needs to know about "now".
At tens of thousands of nodes a week, how would you maintain this report incrementally as node events stream in, including events that arrive late?
A median hides a long tail. Which percentiles would you publish for a customer-facing commitment, and how many clusters does a group need before p95 means anything?

rules.ask: A failed node is replaced and later recovers, so the cluster has one more ready node than it asked for. What does your MAX return, and when was the cluster actually usable?
A node flaps not_ready and back to ready. How many times does your count see it, and can a partial cluster look ready?
Why might the provisioning team prefer the median here, and what would you show next to it so the tail is not hidden?
A customer cancels after every node became ready. Should that request count as a success in this report, and in a different report?
Which timestamp decides the week, and what happens to a request made at 23:50 on a Sunday?

templates.title: SLA credits — unavailable node-minutes per cluster and month, with maintenance announced in advance excluded
templates.subtopic: interval overlap, de-duplicating overlapping intervals, month splitting, tiered CASE

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud offers customers an availability commitment per cluster and month. When a node is unavailable, the minutes count against availability, except during planned maintenance that was announced far enough ahead. At month end the billing team needs, per cluster, the unavailable node-minutes, the availability, and the credit tier it earns under this exercise's SLA (hypothetical terms; check current docs for any real SLA).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month, cluster_id, customer_id, node_minutes, unavailable_node_minutes, availability_pct, credit_pct for every cluster and every month of the report ({{report_months}}), ordered by month, cluster_id. month is the first day of the month (a date). node_minutes is node_count times the minutes in the month. A node is unavailable for each minute covered by one of its node_outages records (started_at inclusive, ended_at exclusive), except minutes inside a maintenance window of the same cluster (starts_at inclusive, ends_at exclusive) that was announced at least {{notice_hours}} hours before it started (announced_at <= starts_at - {{notice_hours}} hours). availability_pct is 100 × (node_minutes − unavailable) / node_minutes rounded to 3 decimals. credit_pct is 0 when that availability (unrounded) is at least {{sla}}, 10 when it is at least 99.0, 25 when it is at least 95.0, and 50 otherwise. {{months_rule}} {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every timestamp is a whole minute, in UTC. The sample has {{outages}} outage records; a real fleet has many thousands of nodes per month.
sections.assumptions: The SLA target, notice period and credit tiers are this exercise's hypothetical rules, not any provider's terms; check current docs. A cluster's node count is constant over the report. Only outage records make a node unavailable; a maintenance window with no outage in it costs nothing.
sections.criteria: Minutes inside advance-announced windows of the same cluster excluded, inclusive notice; overlapping records counted once; outages split at month boundaries and clipped to the report; a cluster × month grid including clusters with no outages; exact tier comparison and an inclusive target; rounding to 3 decimals only for display; deterministic order; a credible plan for interval arithmetic at scale and late records.

clarifications.q: A window was announced exactly {{notice_hours}} hours before it started. Is that in advance?
clarifications.a: Yes. At least the notice period, inclusive.

clarifications.q: An outage starts before a maintenance window and ends inside it.
clarifications.a: Only its minutes inside an advance-announced window are excluded; the rest count.

clarifications.q: Two records cover the same minute on the same node.
clarifications.a: That node-minute is unavailable once.

clarifications.q: Does a maintenance window on one cluster excuse an outage on another?
clarifications.a: No. Only the cluster's own windows apply.

clarifications.q: Is availability exactly at {{sla}} a breach?
clarifications.a: No. At least the target earns no credit; compare before rounding.

hints: The simplest correct shape is a minute grid: expand each outage into its minutes with generate_series, drop minutes inside a qualifying window, and DISTINCT on (node, minute).
Build the cluster × month grid separately and count each cluster's unavailable minutes inside each month's half-open range, so a cluster with no outages still gets a row.
Compare availability with the tiers as 100.0 * (node_minutes - unavailable) >= target * node_minutes to stay exact.
followups: The minute grid is fine for a sample. At 50 000 nodes and month-long outages it is not. Rewrite the unavailable total with interval arithmetic: merge each node's outages, then subtract maintenance overlaps.
A control-plane failure makes the whole cluster unusable while every node reports healthy. How do you model cluster-level unavailability so it is not double counted with node outages?
Credits are paid in the next invoice. An outage record arrives after the month was closed. What do you do with the credit?
Customers ask to audit the number. What do you publish to them, and what must stay out of it?

rules.ask: How many rows does your grid produce for 50 000 nodes in a month with a 3% outage rate, and what would you do instead?
Two monitors recorded the same failure with overlapping records. What does your sum report for that node, and how do you count each minute once?
Is a window announced exactly the notice period ahead in advance or late in your query? Point to the comparison.
Do you choose the credit tier from the rounded or the unrounded availability, and when can the two disagree?
An outage runs from 30 September 22:00 to 1 October 03:00. How many minutes does each month get in your query?

templates.title: Contracted power per data hall and day — peak draw, minutes above 90%, and halls with an hour of missing readings
templates.subtopic: DISTINCT ON de-duplication, local days with AT TIME ZONE, LAG with sentinels for gaps

sections.scenario: Each data hall in a GPU cloud draws power under a contract with a fixed contracted capacity (all figures in this exercise are hypothetical). Meters report a hall's average draw every half hour. The capacity team reviews every hall each day: how close the peak came to the contract, how long the hall ran above 90% of it, and which hall-days cannot be trusted because the meter went quiet for an hour or more.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns day, hall_id, readings, peak_kw, peak_pct, minutes_above_90, data_gap: one row for every hall and every day from {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}, ordered by day, hall_id. A reading at reading_ts (always on :00 or :30) is the hall's average draw over the 30 minutes that start then. A hall's day runs from midnight to midnight in its site_tz, and a reading belongs to the day of its reading_ts in that zone. readings counts the hall-day's readings; peak_kw is the highest draw_kw; peak_pct is 100 × peak_kw / contracted_kw rounded to 1 decimal (both NULL with no readings). minutes_above_90 is 30 for every reading whose draw is strictly greater than 90% of contracted_kw. data_gap is true when some stretch of 60 minutes or more of the day is covered by no reading, including at the start or end of the day. {{days_rule}} {{dup_rule}} {{tz_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A reading of exactly 90% is not above it. A single missing reading leaves 30 uncovered minutes, which is not a gap; two in a row is. The sample has {{readings}} readings.
sections.assumptions: Halls, contracts, draws and time zones are hypothetical. Draws are already in kW; meters never report a reading off the half hour. The report days are in mid-September, with no daylight-saving change.
sections.criteria: De-duplicates by latest received_at; groups by the hall's local day; a hall × day grid that keeps days with no readings; strict 90% comparison; gaps of 60 minutes or more detected at the edges as well as between readings, and a single missing reading not flagged; correct rounding; deterministic order; sensible answers on finer readings, dual feeds and DST days.

clarifications.q: Is a draw of exactly 90% of the contract "above 90%"?
clarifications.a: No. Strictly greater only.

clarifications.q: The first reading of the day is at 01:00. Is that a gap?
clarifications.a: Yes. 00:00 to 01:00 is 60 minutes with no reading covering it.

clarifications.q: One reading is missing at 14:30. Gap?
clarifications.a: No. That is 30 uncovered minutes.

clarifications.q: What if a hall has no readings at all on a day?
clarifications.a: It still gets a row: readings 0, peak_kw and peak_pct NULL, minutes_above_90 0, data_gap true.

clarifications.q: The same reading appears twice with different values.
clarifications.a: Keep the copy with the latest received_at; the meter re-sent a corrected value.

hints: De-duplicate first: DISTINCT ON (hall_id, reading_ts) … ORDER BY hall_id, reading_ts, received_at DESC.
reading_ts AT TIME ZONE site_tz gives local wall-clock time; its ::date is the hall's day. Build the hall × day grid with generate_series and LEFT JOIN onto it.

For gaps, add two sentinel marks per hall-day, 30 minutes before midnight and at the next midnight, then look at t - LAG(t) over the reading starts: a difference of 90 minutes or more means at least 60 uncovered minutes.
followups: The contract is measured on a 15-minute average, not a 30-minute one, and meters move to 1-minute readings. What changes in the query and in what you can claim about the peak?
Halls have two independent feeds whose draws add up, and one feed's meter goes quiet. How do you report the hall's draw honestly?
Turn the daily report into an alert that fires within minutes when a hall runs above 90% for half an hour, without paging on a single noisy reading.
A site in a zone with daylight saving has a 23-hour and a 25-hour day each year. What happens to your grid, your gap rule and minutes_above_90 on those days?

rules.ask: Your LAG compares consecutive readings. What does it say about a hall whose first reading of the day is at 01:30?
A reading is exactly 90% of the contract. Does your query count it, and which rule asks for?
A hall is seven hours behind UTC. Which local day does its reading at 03:00 UTC belong to in your query?
Two copies of a reading have the same received_at. Which one does your query keep, and is that deterministic?
Why does a hall-day with no readings need a grid, and what would your query return for it without one?

templates.title: Maintenance slots — the fewest moments that fall inside every customer's allowed window
templates.subtopic: interval stabbing by earliest end, bisect over merged freezes

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud needs to apply a disruptive update to a shared component that every customer cluster in a region depends on. Each customer cluster has an allowed maintenance window, and the update can be applied at an instant (a "moment") that serves every cluster whose window contains it. Every moment costs a status-page announcement and on-call cover, so the operations team wants as few moments as possible, and, among equally small plans, the latest ones, to leave customers the most time.
sections.problem: Implement maintenance_moments(windows, freezes=()). windows is a list of (start, end) integer minutes, inclusive at both ends, in any order. Return the moments as an ascending list of integers such that every window contains at least one moment, with as few moments as possible. If several smallest schedules exist, return the latest one: compare schedules moment by moment from the first, and the later moment wins at the first difference. Return [] when there are no windows. {{invalid_rule}} {{freeze_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 windows over a year of minutes (525 600) in the timing check, needing thousands of moments. Rebuilding the list of uncovered windows after each pick is O(n·k) and too slow; O(n log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Windows, freezes and minutes are hypothetical; a real maintenance plan also weighs duration, capacity and customer impact. A moment takes no time. Windows are independent of one another, and any minute is a possible moment unless a freeze forbids it.
sections.criteria: Earliest-end greedy with a correct "already served" test (start ≤ last moment); inclusive ends, touching windows sharing a moment; the latest schedule among the smallest; [] for no windows; at Hard, zero-length, duplicate and nested windows and None for an invalid window; at Very Hard, the latest allowed minute under merged freezes and None when a window has none; O(n log n) with a clear argument; an exchange-argument proof sketch.

clarifications.q: Do the windows include their end minute?
clarifications.a: Yes. (10, 20) contains both 10 and 20, so (10, 20) and (20, 30) share the moment 20.

clarifications.q: Are the windows sorted?
clarifications.a: No. They come in any order and may repeat.

clarifications.q: Which schedule do you want when several have the fewest moments?
clarifications.a: The latest: the later first moment wins; if equal, the later second moment, and so on.

clarifications.q: What do I return for an empty list of windows?
clarifications.a: [].

clarifications.q: Can I raise an exception on bad input?
clarifications.a: No. Return None for the cases the statement names.

hints: Look at the window that ends first. Some moment must be inside it, and no moment inside it can be later than its end.
Sort by end. Keep the last moment placed; a window whose start is at or before it is already served, otherwise place a new moment at its end.
With freezes, the latest allowed minute at or before an end is found by merging the freezes once and bisecting into their sorted starts.
followups: Prove that the earliest-end greedy uses the fewest moments, and that it also gives the latest schedule.
Each customer now has two or three allowed windows and any one will do. What happens to the problem, and what would you do in practice?
Each moment can update at most c clusters at once. How does the greedy change, and is it still optimal?
Windows arrive as customers edit them during the week. How would you keep the plan up to date without recomputing it from scratch each time?

rules.ask: Try (0, 500), (40, 80), (200, 260) with a start-ordered greedy. How many moments does it place, and where?
After each pick you rebuild the list of remaining windows. How many window checks is that for 100 000 windows and 7 000 picks?
General set cover is hard. What property of intervals on a line makes this case easy?
Why must touching freezes be merged before you step to the minute before one?
What does the heap give you here that one sort by end does not?

templates.title: Burst stretch — the run of consecutive hours where usage most exceeded the reservation
templates.subtopic: maximum subarray (Kadane) with tie rules and resets

sections.scenario: A customer of a GPU cloud reserves a number of GPUs and can burst above the reservation on demand. Hour by hour, usage sometimes exceeds the reservation and sometimes falls below it. When the account team proposes a larger reservation, they want the single stretch of consecutive hours where the customer's usage most exceeded what it had reserved, counting the quiet hours inside the stretch against it, so the proposal rests on one sustained burst rather than scattered spikes.
sections.problem: Implement burst_stretch(usage, reservation). usage[h] is the GPU-hours the customer used in hour h (hours are numbered from 0). reservation is a list of (from_hour, gpus) steps sorted by from_hour, at most one per hour; a step holds until the next one. The net of hour h is usage[h] minus the GPUs reserved in that hour. Return (start_hour, end_hour, net) for the run of consecutive hours, inclusive, whose total net is largest. If several runs share that total, return the shortest; if still tied, the earliest. Return None if no hour's usage exceeds its reservation. {{reservation_rule}} {{missing_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 52 560 hours (six years of hourly usage) in the timing check. Trying every start and end is O(n²), about 1.4 × 10⁹ pairs, and too slow even with prefix sums. One pass, O(n), is expected.
sections.assumptions: Reservations and usage are hypothetical; how a real contract prices bursts is not part of this exercise. Usage is whole GPU-hours. The run is chosen on net GPU-hours only, not on cost.
sections.criteria: Net per hour from the step in force, 0 before the first step; a one-pass maximum-subarray scan; restart on a non-positive total so ties go to the shortest run; strict improvement for the earliest; None when no hour bursts; at Very Hard, missing hours end every run; O(n) with a clear argument; good answers on bounded length, streaming and top-k.

clarifications.q: Does an hour exactly at the reservation count as bursting?
clarifications.a: No. Its net is 0. If no hour has a positive net, return None.

clarifications.q: Should the run include zero-net hours at its edges?
clarifications.a: Not if it does not have to: among runs with the same total, the shortest wins.

clarifications.q: Two separate bursts have the same total and the same length.
clarifications.a: The earlier one.

clarifications.q: Can the run contain hours below the reservation?
clarifications.a: Yes, if the hours on both sides make up for them; the total net is what is compared.

clarifications.q: May I return a list instead of a tuple?
clarifications.a: Return a tuple (start_hour, end_hour, net), or None.

hints: Keep the best total of a run ending at the current hour: either extend the previous run or start fresh here.
Start fresh whenever the running total is zero or below. Restarting on zero, not only on a negative total, is what keeps the run as short as possible.
Update the answer only when the total is strictly larger, or equal and shorter; that keeps the earliest among equals.
followups: Prove that the restart-on-non-positive rule gives, for each end hour, the shortest run with the best total ending there.
The account team wants the best stretch of at most 72 hours. What changes, and what is the complexity now?
Usage arrives as a stream, hour by hour, for 10 000 customers. What state do you keep per customer to report the best stretch so far?
The team now wants the top three non-overlapping stretches. How would you find them?

rules.ask: How many (start, end) pairs is that for six years of hours, and what would let you skip all but one start per end?
With nets 0, 0, 5, which run does your code return, and which does the tie rule ask for?
Your max over a slice runs in C. What is the total work over all starts, and roughly how long is that for 52 560 hours?
Why is treating a missing hour as zero usage wrong here, and what does your code do instead?
Write the vectorised version: which running minimum do you need alongside the cumulative sum, and how do you keep the tie rule?

templates.title: Accepting GPU reservations in order against a pool's hourly capacity
templates.subtopic: lazy propagation, range add and range minimum over an hourly book

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud sells capacity reservations: a customer asks for a number of GPUs of one type, in one region, for a range of hours that can start months ahead and last for years. Requests for {{pool}} reach the reservation book in the order they are submitted, and each gets an answer straight away. A request is accepted only if, in every hour of its range, the GPUs already booked plus the new request stay within the pool's capacity for that hour. Otherwise it is rejected whole, with nothing booked. Customers can also cancel a reservation, which frees its GPUs for later requests. The book is hourly and covers several years.
sections.problem: Implement accept_reservations(horizon, capacity, ops). The book covers hours 0 to horizon - 1. capacity is a list of (from_hour, gpus) steps, sorted by hour, the first at hour 0; each step holds until the next one. ops is processed in order. ("reserve", rid, start, end, gpus) asks for gpus GPUs in every hour of [start, end): end is exclusive. It is accepted when, for every hour h in the range, the GPUs booked at h by accepted, uncancelled reservations plus gpus is at most the capacity at h. ("cancel", rid) releases reservation rid if it is accepted and not yet cancelled. Return one bool per op, in order: for a reservation, whether it was accepted; for a cancellation, whether it released something. A cancellation of a rejected, unknown or already cancelled id returns False and changes nothing. Every rid in a reserve op is unique. {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check has 60 000 ops on a book of 52 560 hours (six years), with requests lasting between a year and a half and four and a half years. Checking or updating every hour of every request is billions of steps in CPython, and even a min() over a list slice copies tens of thousands of values per request. Something close to O(log horizon) per op, after an O(horizon) setup, is expected.
sections.assumptions: Pools, capacities, request sizes and the six-year book are hypothetical; how real reservations are sold, sized and cancelled is not described here, so check current docs. One pool means one GPU type in one region. GPUs in a pool are interchangeable, so only the count per hour matters, not which machines. Hours are whole UTC hours.
sections.criteria: Half-open ranges; a request accepted only if every hour fits, at exactly capacity included; rejected requests book nothing; cancellations release only accepted, uncancelled reservations and return False otherwise; malformed requests rejected at Hard and Very Hard; capacity steps, including a step to 0, honoured at Very Hard; headroom with range minimum and range add in O(log horizon) per op (a lazy segment tree, or a block decomposition argued carefully); a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on largest fit, earliest start and concurrent acceptance.

clarifications.q: Is end part of the reservation?
clarifications.a: No. [start, end) books hours start to end - 1, so a reservation ending at hour 10 and one starting at hour 10 never overlap.

clarifications.q: Can a request be partly accepted, for the hours that fit?
clarifications.a: No. It is accepted for its whole range or rejected with nothing booked.

clarifications.q: Does a rejected request change anything for later requests?
clarifications.a: No. Only accepted reservations book GPUs.

clarifications.q: What does a cancellation of something that was rejected return?
clarifications.a: False, and the book does not change. The same goes for an unknown id and a second cancellation.

clarifications.q: Can a planned reduction leave a pool over capacity?
clarifications.a: No. Steps are known before the first request, so every check already uses them.

clarifications.q: Are the requests sorted by start hour?
clarifications.a: No. They arrive in submission order, and that order decides who gets the capacity.

hints: Keep the headroom per hour: capacity minus GPUs booked. A request fits exactly when the minimum headroom over its range is at least its size.
You need two operations over a range: the minimum, and adding a value to every hour. Which structure does both in logarithmic time?

A segment tree over hours with a pending add stored on internal nodes (lazy propagation). A reservation adds -gpus to its range, a cancellation adds +gpus, and the leaves start from the capacity steps.
followups: A rejected customer asks for the largest number of GPUs they could have over the same hours. How does your structure answer that with one query?
A rejected request may move: find the earliest start at or after the requested one where the same duration and size fit. How would you descend the tree to find it faster than trying every start?
Requests can be placed in either of two regions with different prices. Which rule decides, and what extra state would you keep so the choice can be explained to the customer later?
Several API servers accept requests for the same pool at once. How do you keep decisions consistent with submission order, and what do you persist so the book survives a restart?

rules.ask: A request spans four years. How many steps does one check take, and how many for 60 000 requests?
The minimum over a slice runs in C, but what does copying a 30 000-hour slice cost, and how do you update the booked counts afterwards?
Why must a pending add be pushed down, or added on the way up, before you trust a child's minimum? Show a request that goes wrong if you skip it.
Which block size do you pick for 52 560 hours, and how does the cost per request compare with a tree?
You keep accepted reservations as sorted intervals. How do you get the busiest hour inside a new request's range from them?

templates.title: Private interconnect plan: the cheapest links joining a customer's clusters
templates.subtopic: minimum spanning tree, Kruskal with union-find, a strict tie rule

sections.scenario: A customer runs several GPU clusters across sites and regions and wants them joined by private links, so that every cluster can reach every other one directly or through other clusters. A planning tool lists the candidate links the provider could set up, each with a hypothetical monthly cost. The tool must propose the cheapest set of links that joins every cluster, show its monthly total, and give the same answer every time it is run on the same input, so that a quote never changes between two runs.
sections.problem: Implement interconnect_plan(clusters, links, existing=()). clusters is a list of distinct cluster ids. links is a list of (link_id, cluster_a, cluster_b, monthly_cost): a link joins its two clusters in both directions, and monthly_cost is a positive integer. A plan is a set of links such that every cluster can reach every other one through links of the plan. Return (total_cost, ids) for the cheapest plan, where ids is the sorted list of its link ids. When several plans share the lowest total, compare links by (monthly_cost, link_id), with link ids compared as strings: under that order no two links tie, and the answer is the plan that is cheapest under it, which is unique. If there is a single cluster, return (0, []). {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check is a stress test with 8 000 clusters and 100 000 candidate links. Adding links in cost order and running a search over the chosen links to test each one is O(E·(V + E)) and takes minutes. Something close to O(E log E) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Clusters, sites, links and costs are hypothetical; how private networking is really priced or provisioned is not described here, so check current docs. Every link has the same capacity, so cost is the only thing that matters. The input can contain many links of equal cost.
sections.criteria: The cheapest plan with n − 1 links; the (monthly_cost, link_id) tie rule applied, so equal-cost inputs give one answer; sorted ids and the right total; one cluster gives (0, []); at Hard and Very Hard, self-links and unknown clusters ignored, parallel links handled and None when no plan exists; at Very Hard, existing links counted as joined and never returned; Kruskal with union-find (or Prim with a heap keyed by the same order) rather than a search per link; a clear argument for why the greedy choice is safe; sensible answers on redundancy, cost changes and bandwidth.

clarifications.q: Do two clusters need a direct link?
clarifications.a: No. A path through other clusters is enough.

clarifications.q: Which plan do I return when two have the same total?
clarifications.a: The one the (monthly_cost, link_id) order prefers. It is the same as raising every cost by a tiny amount that grows with the link id, which makes the cheapest plan unique.

clarifications.q: Are link ids zero-padded?
clarifications.a: Yes, they have a fixed width, so comparing them as strings and as numbers agree.

clarifications.q: What if a link names the same cluster twice?
clarifications.a: It joins nothing, so it is never part of a plan. That only happens where the statement says so.

clarifications.q: Must ids be in the order I chose the links?
clarifications.a: No. Return them sorted.

hints: A cheapest plan never contains a cycle: dropping the most expensive link of a cycle keeps everything joined and costs less. So a plan for n clusters has n − 1 links.
Take links from cheapest to most expensive and keep a link only if its two clusters are not yet joined. Why is that safe?
"Are these two clusters already joined?" is a union-find question. Use path compression (or halving) and union by size or rank, and stop once one group remains.
followups: The customer wants every cluster to stay reachable if any single link fails. What changes in the problem, and what would you propose?
One link's monthly cost drops after the plan is made. How do you update the plan without rebuilding it from scratch?
Links now have bandwidth, and traffic between some pairs of clusters must fit. Why is the cheapest plan no longer enough, and how would you approach it?
The customer adds a rule that no two clusters may be more than three links apart. How does that change the difficulty, and what would you do in practice?

rules.ask: You search the chosen links for every candidate. How many searches is that at 100 000 links, and how big does each get?
Which optimisations do you use, and what does a find cost without them after a long chain of unions?
Your heap is keyed by cost. When two links cost the same, does your key give the same plan as the tie rule? Show why.
A shortest-path tree from one cluster minimises the distance from that cluster, not the total cost. Give a small example where the two differ.
The customer gets None. How would you tell them which clusters cannot be reached, and which link they would need to order?

templates.title: Debug the GPU-hour invoice calculator
templates.subtopic: per-second metering, reserved hours per month, price amendments, month boundaries, rounding once

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud bills GPU instances by the second. Customers with a reservation get a number of GPU-hours each month at a reserved rate, and usage beyond that is billed at the on-demand rate, which can be amended in the middle of a month. Finance and customers have reported several problems with the monthly invoice lines. A training job that ran for three days was billed for a few hours. A customer's reserved hours seem to run out in their second month. A run that started before a price change was billed entirely at the old price. Usage from the first hours of a month appears on the previous month's invoice. Totals are sometimes a cent off from the customer's own calculation. The calculator below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix monthly_invoice_lines(runs, prices, reservations) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Runs. runs are dicts {"customer", "gpu_type", "gpus", "start", "end"} for instance runs. start and end are ISO 8601 timestamps in UTC with whole seconds, and end is at or after start. A run's usage is gpus times its length in seconds: metering is per second (this exercise's rule).
  2. Months. Usage belongs to the calendar month in UTC in which it happened. A run across a month boundary is split at the boundary.
  3. On-demand prices. prices are dicts {"gpu_type", "from", "cents_per_hour"}: the on-demand price per GPU-hour from from until that type's next row. Usage is priced at the row in force when it happened, so a run across an amendment is split at it. Every run starts after its type's first row.
  4. Reserved hours. reservations maps "<customer>|<gpu_type>" to {"hours", "cents_per_hour"}. Each calendar month, the first hours GPU-hours of that customer's usage of that type are billed at the reserved rate, and the rest at on-demand prices. Reserved hours cover the month's earliest price period first. Unused reserved hours do not carry over. A customer and type with no entry pays on-demand prices for everything.
  5. Output. A dict keyed "<customer>|<YYYY-MM>|<gpu_type>" for every line with usage, each value {"gpu_seconds", "reserved_seconds", "on_demand_seconds", "amount_cents"}. amount_cents is the exact amount of the line, reserved GPU-seconds times the reserved rate plus each period's on-demand GPU-seconds times its rate, divided by 3 600 and rounded once, half up, to a whole cent.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Keep money exact: integers until the single rounding. Up to 100 000 runs, processed in close to linear time.
sections.assumptions: Prices, reservations, customers and the per-second rule are hypothetical; how any real GPU cloud meters, prices and rounds is not described here, so check current docs. A reservation's rate and hours do not change within the data. Months are cut in UTC.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its finance or customer symptom; usage metered for every second of a run, including whole days; reserved hours reset each month; each piece of a run priced at the rate in force when it happened and billed to the month it happened in; one rounding per line, half up, on an exact integer amount; minimal fixes that keep the output format; a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Which price applies to a run that crosses an amendment?
clarifications.a: Each part at its own price: the seconds before the amendment at the old price, the seconds after at the new one.

clarifications.q: Do unused reserved hours roll into the next month?
clarifications.a: No. Every month starts with the full hours, used or not.

clarifications.q: When reserved hours run out in the middle of a month with two prices, which seconds become on-demand?
clarifications.a: The later ones. Reserved hours cover the earliest price period first.

clarifications.q: How is half a cent rounded?
clarifications.a: Up. 2.5 cents is 3 cents. And the line is rounded once, not each part of it.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Feed the calculator one run of two days and three hours and read the GPU-seconds it reports.
Follow the variable that holds the remaining reserved seconds from one invoice line to the next. What is it keyed by?
Inside the loop over a run's pieces, which variables describe the piece and which describe the whole run?
Work out a 36-second run at 250 cents per GPU-hour by hand, then read every round.
followups: A price amendment is announced after the month has started and backdated to its first day. Which invoice lines change, and what does the customer see?
A customer disputes a line. What would you store with each invoice line so support can rebuild it second by second?
Usage records arrive up to a day late from some regions. When is a month's invoice final, and how do you issue a correction after that?
Reservations become pooled across GPU types at different conversion rates. How would the allocation of reserved hours change, and which order would you choose?

rules.ask: What does timedelta(days=2, hours=3).seconds return, and where else in a billing system could the same mistake hide?
Where does the remaining reserved allowance live, and what key would make it impossible to leak from one month into the next?
Python's round(2.5) is 2. Which rounding rule does your fix use, and how do you keep the amount exact until you apply it?
Where could a float enter this calculation, and what is the largest line amount before an error in the last cent is possible?
A run crosses both a month end and an amendment within the same hour. Walk through how your loop splits it.

templates.title: Object storage request logs into per-customer usage
templates.subtopic: log ingestion, late batches, deduplication, daily billable totals

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud also sells object storage, used for training data, checkpoints and model artefacts. Customers are billed per day for the bytes stored in each storage class ({{storage_classes}}), for requests by kind, and for bytes read out. About {{daily_requests}} requests a day pass through {{gateways}} storage gateways, each writing request logs in batches. Most batches land within minutes, but a gateway that loses its connection can deliver a batch up to {{late_hours}} hours late, and a retried upload can deliver the same batch twice. Finance wants daily billable totals per customer, bucket and storage class that match the invoice, and customers want to see their own usage the next morning.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from gateway request logs to daily billable usage per customer. Cover the log record and batch format, how batches are ingested and deduplicated, how late batches reach past days, how stored bytes per day are computed (from requests, from bucket snapshots, or both), how requests and bytes read are counted by kind and class, when a day is final and how corrections are issued, and how each customer sees only its own usage.
sections.constraints: A batch delivered twice must never be billed twice. A day's totals must be re-runnable and give the same answer. Late batches up to {{late_hours}} hours must land on the day the requests happened. Stored bytes must account for objects that are overwritten, deleted or moved between classes. Object keys and contents are customer data: the pipeline uses sizes, classes and request kinds, never object contents.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, gateway counts, storage classes and lateness are hypothetical, and so is any billing rule; check current docs for real pricing and metering. Each gateway numbers its batches. Every request carries a bucket id and the server's timestamp. Buckets belong to exactly one customer.
sections.criteria: Batch identity and an applied-batch record for idempotent ingestion; event-time days with late batches rewriting their day's partition; a stated definition of stored bytes with a size ledger or inventory reconciliation; overwrites, deletes and class changes handled; billable status rules; a finality rule and versioned corrections; per-customer isolation and no object contents in the pipeline; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is stored bytes per day the bytes at midnight, or an average?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but say it, and keep it consistent between the invoice and what customers see. A time-weighted average (byte-hours) is common.

clarifications.q: Can a request log tell us an object's size after an overwrite?
clarifications.a: The PUT logs the new size; the old size is only known if you kept it. That is part of the design.

clarifications.q: Which timestamp decides the day?
clarifications.a: The gateway's request timestamp in UTC, not the arrival time of the batch.

clarifications.q: Do failed requests count?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, requests that the service rejected with a server error are not billable; client errors are. Keep the status in the record.

hints: Make every batch identifiable (gateway id plus sequence number) and record which batches have been applied, so a replay is a no-op.
Request counts and bytes read are additive per day. Stored bytes are a state: derive them from a per-object size ledger, or reconcile against a daily bucket inventory.
Write daily totals as partitions you can rebuild: when a late batch arrives, recompute that day's partition, not a running counter.
followups: A gateway's clock drifts by two hours for a day. How would you detect it, and which days' totals move when you fix it?
A customer moves a petabyte from one class to another in an hour. How does your stored-bytes calculation treat that day?
A late batch arrives after the month's invoice was issued. What do you do, and what does the customer see?
Volume grows to ten times {{daily_requests}} a day. Which stage breaks first, and how do you scale it?

rules.ask: Where exactly is the duplicate batch dropped, and what proves to finance that it was?
The daily inventory and the request-derived bytes disagree by 0.3% for one bucket. Which do you bill, and how do you investigate?
A batch from yesterday 23:50 arrives today at 03:00. Which day does it bill to, and when do you consider yesterday final?
A batch is replayed after a crash halfway through. How do your counters avoid counting part of it twice?
Why do you need that field for billing, and who could read it in the analytics tables?

incidents: A gateway restarts with its batch sequence reset to 1, and its new batches are dropped as duplicates of old ones for six hours.
After a network outage, one site's gateways deliver {{late_hours}} hours of batches at once, and the day's totals for its customers change after customers have already looked at them.
A lifecycle rule moves millions of objects to a colder class overnight, and stored bytes for both classes are counted for the whole day.

templates.title: Cluster provisioning telemetry: from request to ready
templates.subtopic: state machines, stuck-request detection, customer-facing status

sections.scenario: Customers of a GPU cloud create Kubernetes-based clusters and add node pools of GPU nodes, up to {{max_nodes}} nodes in one request. A request moves through stages: capacity allocated, nodes imaged, health checks passed, nodes joined to the cluster, and the request ready. There are about {{daily_requests}} provisioning requests a day across {{regions}} regions. Customers see a status page for each request, operators want to find requests that are stuck (no progress for {{stuck_minutes}} minutes), and the product team wants weekly reports of time to ready by region and GPU type.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry for cluster and node-pool provisioning. Cover the events each stage emits for the request and for each node, the state model and its allowed transitions, how a request's state is derived from its nodes' states, how out-of-order and duplicate events are handled, how stuck requests and stuck nodes are detected and alerted on, what the customer sees and how often it updates, and the tables behind the weekly time-to-ready reports.
sections.constraints: Status shown to a customer must never go backwards because of an out-of-order event. A request for {{max_nodes}} nodes must not need {{max_nodes}} separate status lookups to render. Stuck detection must fire within a few minutes of the {{stuck_minutes}}-minute threshold and must not page on requests that are waiting on purpose, for example for capacity a customer agreed to wait for. Customers see only their own requests. Reports must handle requests cancelled part-way.
sections.assumptions: Stage names, volumes, thresholds and region counts are hypothetical; this exercise does not describe how any real provider provisions clusters, so check current docs. Each node and each request has a stable id. Components emit events with their own timestamps, and clocks can disagree by seconds.
sections.criteria: Per-node state machines with versioned, idempotent transitions; request state derived from node counts and never moving backwards on stale events; stuck detection based on progress, with deliberate waits excluded; customer status that is fast, aggregated and isolated per customer; an append-only log and report tables that treat cancelled and partial requests explicitly; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: When is a request ready: all nodes, or enough of them?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, when every node requested is ready, or when the customer accepted a partial cluster. Record which.

clarifications.q: Can a node go back from health checks to imaging?
clarifications.a: Yes, when a check fails and the node is re-imaged or replaced. That is progress, not a regression of the request.

clarifications.q: What is a stuck request?
clarifications.a: One where no node has moved forward for {{stuck_minutes}} minutes and the request is not in a deliberate waiting state.

clarifications.q: Do customers see per-node detail?
clarifications.a: They see counts per stage and a reason for any node that failed, never other customers' information or internal host names.

hints: Make each node a small state machine with versioned transitions, and derive the request's state from counts of nodes per stage rather than storing it independently.
Separate "the last time anything progressed" from "the last event received", and drive stuck detection from the first.
Keep an append-only event log for reporting, and a current-state table keyed by request for the status page.
followups: A health-check component restarts and re-sends every result from the last hour. What does your design do with them?
Customers ask for an estimated time to ready. What data would you use, and how would you avoid promising too much?
Time to ready for one region doubles overnight. How would you find which stage is responsible?
At {{daily_requests}} requests a day with {{max_nodes}}-node pools, which part of the pipeline is the bottleneck, and how do you scale it?

rules.ask: A "joined" event arrives before "health checks passed" for the same node. What does your state machine do, and what does the customer see?
How often does the status page poll, and what does that cost at {{daily_requests}} requests a day?
A request waits for capacity on purpose for three hours. How does your stuck detector know not to page?
Do cancelled and partial requests enter your time-to-ready percentiles? Which choice could hide a problem?
Events for one node land on two partitions. How do you keep its transitions in order?

incidents: An imaging service bug marks nodes imaged twice, and status pages show some requests jumping back to an earlier stage for an hour.
Stuck alerts fire for hundreds of requests in one region that are correctly waiting for capacity, and the on-call engineer mutes the alert for the night.
A pool of {{max_nodes}} nodes has one node that never passes health checks, and the customer's request has shown 99% for {{stuck_minutes}} minutes without a reason.

templates.title: Contracts and reservations as data — ramps, amendments and committed capacity as of a date
templates.subtopic: contract versions, ramp schedules, valid time versus knowledge time, capacity holds

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud sells capacity two ways: on-demand instances by the hour, and reserved capacity under contracts. In this exercise's model, a contract has one or more lines; each line commits a number of GPUs of one GPU type in one region for a term of up to {{term_years}} years, at a price per GPU-hour, and usually ramps up in steps (up to {{max_ramp_steps}} steps per line) as the provider brings capacity online and the customer grows into it. Contracts change: a contract is amended about {{amendments_per_year}} times a year on average, to add GPUs, move a ramp step earlier or later, add a region, or change the price from a future month. Behind each line, the provider holds physical capacity for the customer (a capacity reservation) in a region or availability zone, which may be in place before the line starts. There are about {{active_contracts}} active contracts. Sales, finance, capacity planning and provisioning all ask "how many GPUs are committed on this date?", and they do not always mean the same thing. All prices, terms and counts are hypothetical.
sections.problem: Design the data model for contracts and reservations. Cover: the contract, its lines and its amendments, and what an amendment stores (the whole restated terms, or only the changes); ramp steps and prices per line, with money as integer minor units and a currency; the capacity reservations that hold supply for each line and how they relate to the commitment; and the two times every question needs, when a term applies (the day it commits GPUs) and when it was agreed (the amendment's signing). Show how to answer: "committed GPUs by GPU type, region and day for next quarter, as the contracts stand today"; "what did this contract commit for last March, as it stood when March was invoiced"; and "lines whose reservations hold fewer GPUs than they commit".
sections.constraints: An amendment never overwrites earlier terms; any past state of a contract can be reconstructed. A line's GPU type and region are fixed; moving GPUs to another region ends part of one line and starts another. Prices are integer minor units per GPU-hour with a currency, and a price change applies only from its stated effective date. A customer sees only its own contracts.
sections.assumptions: Contract counts, steps, amendment rates, terms, prices and GPU types are hypothetical; check current docs for how any real offering is contracted. On-demand usage is out of scope except where a contract states a rate for use above its commitment (this exercise's rule).
sections.criteria: Contract and line identity separated from immutable amendments and the terms they restate; ramp steps and prices per line with effective dates and integer minor units; valid time and knowledge time both modelled, with "as it stood on a date" answerable; region moves and renewals modelled without double counting; reservations distinct from commitments, with a reconciliation between them; a derived daily committed-capacity table with a stated rebuild trigger; customer-level access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can an amendment change a date in the past?
clarifications.a: Yes. By agreement a ramp step can be back-dated, for example to the day capacity was actually handed over. Finance still needs to see what was agreed before the amendment.

clarifications.q: Does a contract have one GPU type?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily. A contract can have several lines, each with its own GPU type, region, ramp and price.

clarifications.q: Is a capacity reservation the same thing as the commitment?
clarifications.a: No. The commitment is what the customer bought; the reservation is supply the provider holds for it. A reservation can start before the line, cover only part of it, or move between zones.

clarifications.q: What does a renewal look like?
clarifications.a: Your choice: a new contract or an amendment extending the term. State the choice and what it does to the commitment in the overlap month.

clarifications.q: How precise must prices be?
clarifications.a: Exact. Integer minor units per GPU-hour, with the currency; no floating point.

hints: Separate identity (contract, line) from versions (amendment, signed on a date) from terms (ramp steps and prices that each amendment restates).
Two time axes: the effective date of a step says when it applies; the amendment's signing date says when it became known. A question "as it stood on date K" filters amendments by signing date first.
Derive a daily committed-capacity table from the terms instead of storing counters that amendments must keep in sync.
followups: Write the query shape for committed GPUs by GPU type, region and day next quarter as the contracts stand today, and the same as they stood on the first of last month. What changes between the two?
A customer moves 64 GPUs from one region to another in month 7 of a {{term_years}}-year term. Model it, and show both regions' committed GPUs for months 6 to 8.
An amendment back-dates a ramp step by two weeks. Which reports change, which must not, and how does an invoice already sent stay explainable?

With {{active_contracts}} contracts, up to {{max_ramp_steps}} steps per line and about {{amendments_per_year}} amendments per contract a year, estimate a daily committed-capacity table over the whole horizon. Do you materialise it, and what triggers a rebuild?

rules.ask: Finance asks what the contract committed for March as it stood when March was invoiced, before last week's amendment. Can your model answer that?
Capacity planning needs committed GPUs by type, region and day across every contract. How do they query terms stored inside documents, and what validates them?
Does your validity range say when a term applies or when it was agreed? Walk through a back-dated ramp step with it.
A price changes with a ramp step, and an amendment changes it again from a future month. Where does the price live, and how does an invoice pick the right one?
The provider holds capacity in a zone for a line that starts next month. Is that a commitment, a reservation or both, and how does capacity planning avoid counting it twice?

incidents: An amendment that moved a ramp step two weeks earlier was entered by editing the step's date in place. The quarter's committed-capacity report changed silently, and last month's invoice for that contract no longer matches the terms shown to the customer.

A renewal was loaded as a new contract while the old contract's last month was still running. With about {{amendments_per_year}} amendments per contract a year already flowing through the same pipeline, nobody noticed that the capacity forecast counted the renewing customers' GPUs twice for the overlap month.
A region's GPUs were moved to another zone, but the capacity reservations still pointed at the old zone. The report of lines held below their commitment listed dozens of healthy lines for a week.

templates.title: Customer clusters as data — node pools, node lifecycle and the reservation each node counts against
templates.subtopic: declared versus observed state, lifecycle events, interval attribution to reservations

sections.scenario: Customers of a GPU cloud run managed, Kubernetes-based clusters (described generally here). A cluster has node pools; each pool declares an instance type (a GPU type and node size) and a target node count up to {{max_pool_nodes}}, and the service works to bring the running count to the declared count. A node goes through requested, provisioning, ready, draining and released; a node that fails a health check is replaced by a new node. Each ready node counts against one of the customer's capacity reservations for that GPU type and region, or, when none has room, is billed on demand (this exercise's rule). There are about {{clusters}} clusters, about {{lifecycle_events}} lifecycle events a day, and about {{replacement_share}} of nodes are replaced each week. Customers see their own clusters' state and history; finance needs node-hours by reservation and by on-demand use.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: clusters, node pools and their declared settings over time (instance type, target count, labels); nodes and their lifecycle as events, and how the current state and any past state are derived; replacements, and how a replacement is linked to the node it replaced; the attribution of each ready node to a reservation or to on-demand use as time intervals; and the tables that answer "nodes ready per pool at a given minute", "minutes from request to ready by GPU type and region", "the gap between declared and ready nodes per pool over a day" and "node-hours per reservation and on-demand per customer and day".
sections.constraints: Lifecycle events are immutable, can arrive late and out of order, and come from more than one source. A node id is never reused. At any instant a ready node counts against at most one reservation or is on demand, and a reservation never has more GPUs counted against it than it holds. A customer sees only its own clusters.
sections.assumptions: Cluster counts, pool sizes, event volumes and replacement rates are hypothetical. In this exercise a node is billed from ready until released, and draining counts as billed time; check current docs for real billing rules. Reservation terms come from the contracts model and are given.
sections.criteria: Declared pool settings versioned and kept apart from observed lifecycle events; node state as intervals derived from immutable events ordered by source time; replacements as new nodes linked to the one they replaced; attribution to reservations or on demand as intervals with the capacity invariant; measures (ready nodes at a minute, time to ready, declared-versus-ready gap, node-hours by basis) defined on stated grains; storage and query cost reasoned at the stated volumes; customer-level access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a replacement the same node?
clarifications.a: No. It is a new node id that records which node it replaced. Both may be ready for a few minutes at once.

clarifications.q: Who decides which reservation a node counts against?
clarifications.a: An attribution step, by this exercise's rule: the reservation of the matching GPU type and region with room, oldest first; otherwise on demand. When a reservation ends, its nodes move to another reservation or to on demand without being restarted.

clarifications.q: Can a pool's declared count change while nodes are provisioning?
clarifications.a: Yes. Declared settings are versioned, and nodes being provisioned for an older target may be released before they become ready.

clarifications.q: Which time do events carry?
clarifications.a: The time of the transition at the source, and the time it was received. They can differ by minutes.

clarifications.q: Does a customer see other customers' nodes in shared zones?
clarifications.a: Never. Only their own.

hints: Keep declared state (pool settings, versioned) apart from observed state (node lifecycle events). The gap between them is a derived measure, not a stored counter.
Model node state as intervals derived from events ordered by source time, not by arrival.
Attribution is itself a set of intervals per node: (node, reservation or on demand, from, to). Billing and reservation use read those intervals.
followups: Walk one node through requested, provisioning, ready, a failed health check, draining and released, with its replacement. Which rows exist in your model at the end?
A ready event arrives before the provisioning event for the same node. How does your derived state stay right, and what does the customer see in the meantime?
A reservation ends at midnight while 40 of its nodes are running. Show the attribution intervals before and after, and how node-hours for that day split.
At {{lifecycle_events}} events a day across {{clusters}} clusters, what do you store at full grain, what do you derive, and how fast can "ready nodes per pool at a past minute" be answered?

rules.ask: The customer asks how many nodes were ready in a pool at 03:00 yesterday. With a status column updated in place, how do you answer?
Two sources report the same node's transitions, and one is minutes behind. Which time orders your events, and what happens to a state derived by arrival?
A replacement comes up with the same hostname as the node it replaced. What identifies a node in your model, and how are node-hours kept from overlapping?
A node outlives the reservation it started under. With one reservation column on the node, how do you split its node-hours?
The target count drops while nodes are still provisioning. Which nodes are released, and how does your gap measure treat nodes that never became ready?

incidents: A replacement node came up with the same hostname as the node it replaced. With about {{replacement_share}} of nodes replaced each week, node-hours were counted twice for the overlapping minutes and several customers' usage exports disagreed with their clusters' history.

At {{lifecycle_events}} lifecycle events a day, one source began delivering events minutes late. A current-state table updated in arrival order showed thousands of nodes as provisioning hours after they were ready, and the customer status page agreed with it.
A reservation ended at midnight UTC and the attribution step ran only hourly, so an hour of node time across many clusters was attributed to an expired reservation and never billed on demand.

templates.title: Sites as data — regions, halls, power contracts, rack positions and sellable capacity as of a date
templates.subtopic: physical hierarchy, phased power, capacity states, as-of derivations

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud operates in several regions; each region has availability zones, each zone has one or more data centres (some owned, some leased), and each data centre has halls with rack positions. In this exercise's model every number is hypothetical: there are about {{halls}} halls, a hall's power contract allows up to about {{hall_power}} for IT load and is often energised in phases, a dense GPU rack draws about {{rack_power}}, and about {{spare_share}} of installed GPUs are held back as spares for replacements. Racks move through states: planned, delivered, installed, burned in and sellable, held, and out of service. Sales asks how many GPUs of each type can be sold in a region on a date; finance asks what was sellable last quarter; site teams ask which halls are short of power for the racks planned in them.
sections.problem: Design the data model for sites and their capacity. Cover: the hierarchy (region, zone, data centre, hall, rack position) and how it changes over time (halls added, zones re-drawn, positions re-numbered); power contracts and their phases with energisation dates, planned and actual; rack positions with their power and cooling limits; racks, their node type and GPU count, and their state history; spares and held capacity; and the derivation of sellable GPUs by GPU type, region and date, both as planned and as it actually stood. Show how to answer "sellable GPUs by type and region on any past date", "halls where planned rack power exceeds energised power next quarter", and "racks installed but not yet sellable, by age".
sections.constraints: History is never overwritten: last quarter's sellable capacity must reproduce exactly. A rack occupies at most one position at a time, and the power of the racks in a hall never exceeds that hall's energised power. Spares are never counted as sellable. Location details are internal to the provider; customers see only region and zone availability.
sections.assumptions: Halls, power figures, rack draws, spare shares and state names are hypothetical; check current docs for any real region or zone. Power is modelled at the hall level; electrical design within a hall is out of scope. The GPU count of a node type is fixed.
sections.criteria: A hierarchy with validity ranges so past reports reproduce; power contracts in phases with planned and actual dates; rack positions with limits and racks with state intervals; spares and held capacity defined; sellable capacity derived as the lower of installed-and-burned-in and power-supported, as planned and as it stood; location detail kept internal; materialisation reasoned at the stated scale; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a power contract energised all at once?
clarifications.a: Not here. It is energised in phases, each with a planned and an actual date, and a phase can slip.

clarifications.q: When does a rack become sellable?
clarifications.a: After it is installed and passes burn-in, if the hall's energised power covers it. Some sellable racks are then held for a customer's reservation; held racks are still capacity, but not free to sell.

clarifications.q: Can a zone be re-drawn?
clarifications.a: Yes, rarely. A data centre can move to another zone in the provider's model, and past reports must still show the zone as it was then.

clarifications.q: Are spares fixed racks?
clarifications.a: Your choice: designated spare racks, or a share of each hall's GPUs. State it, because it changes how a failed node's replacement is counted.

clarifications.q: Does sellable capacity depend on power or on installed racks?
clarifications.a: Both. The lower of what is installed and burned in, and what the energised power can run, by this exercise's rule.

hints: Treat the hierarchy as slowly changing: positions belong to halls, halls to data centres, data centres to zones, each with validity ranges.
Keep plan and actual apart for power phases and racks; sellable capacity "as planned" and "as it stood" are different derivations from the same tables.
Derive sellable GPUs per day from state intervals and power limits; never store a running total that later corrections must patch.
followups: Write the derivation of sellable GPUs for one hall on one date, from rack state intervals, the energised power phases and the spare rule.
A power phase slips by a quarter. Which reports change, which must not, and how does sales see the new date?
A data centre moves to another zone. Show how last quarter's report by zone still reproduces exactly.
At {{halls}} halls with daily state history for every rack, how large is the daily sellable-capacity table, and what do you materialise for sales to query in under a second?

rules.ask: A rack fails burn-in after its hall's capacity number was updated. How do you correct the number, and how do you reproduce last quarter's figure afterwards?
The contract allows more power than is energised today. Which of the two limits sellable capacity, and where does each live in your model?
A rack is moved to another position in another hall. Does it keep its identity, and which hall's history shows its GPUs for the move day?
A spare node replaces a failed one in a customer's cluster. Does sellable capacity change, and which state records the swap?
The zone boundaries changed last month. Which zone does a report for last quarter use, and how does your model know?

incidents: A hall's second power phase slipped by a quarter, but sellable capacity was computed from the contracted total of about {{hall_power}}. Sales committed racks drawing about {{rack_power}} each that the hall could not yet run.

A re-numbering of rack positions in one data centre was loaded as new positions without closing the old ones. For a month the same GPUs appeared in two halls, and regional sellable capacity was overstated.
One report treated the {{spare_share}} spare holdback as sellable and another did not. Two dashboards disagreed by exactly that share and both were presented in the same planning meeting.

templates.title: Storage and networking services as data — volumes, buckets, networks, addresses and billable units per day
templates.subtopic: resource lifecycles, attachments over time, unit definitions, state-based daily billing

sections.scenario: Besides GPU instances, a GPU cloud sells storage and networking as services: block and shared-file volumes attached to clusters, object storage buckets with storage classes, private networks joining a customer's clusters, and public IP addresses. In this exercise's model, which is hypothetical throughout: a volume is billed on its provisioned size and tier; a bucket on the bytes stored per class each day; a public address while it is allocated to a customer, whether or not it is attached; a private network is free but its attachments are tracked. Billing measures resources {{metering_step}}; a deleted volume is kept recoverable for {{retention_days}} days before it is purged (whether retention is billed is a decision for this design); a released public address can return to the pool and be reassigned to another customer after {{reassign_minutes}} minutes. There are about {{resources}} resources. Customers see their resources and daily billable units; finance needs billable units per customer, service, unit and day.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: each resource type, its identity and lifecycle (created, resized or reclassed, attached and detached, deleted, retained, purged); attachments of volumes, networks and addresses to clusters as time intervals; how stored bytes per bucket and class are captured (state snapshots versus change events) and corrected; the definition of each billable unit (GB-days, GB-month equivalents, address-hours) and the rule for partial intervals; and the fact table of billable units per customer, resource, unit and day that invoices are built from. Show how a customer can trace one day's charge for one volume back to the lifecycle rows that produced it.
sections.constraints: Lifecycle history is immutable and every billable quantity is derived from it. Two customers never hold the same address at the same instant, and an address's charges go to the customer who held it at that instant. Units are exact: integers in a stated base unit (bytes, minutes), converted once when invoiced. A customer sees only its own resources.
sections.assumptions: Resource counts, metering step, retention and reassignment times, tiers and storage classes are hypothetical; check current docs for any real price or rule. Prices are out of scope; the design stops at billable units. Object request logs and network transfer metering are covered elsewhere and are out of scope here.
sections.criteria: Resource identity separated from append-only state intervals; attachments as their own intervals; snapshot versus event capture reasoned, with one authoritative source and a correction path; units defined in base units with one partial-interval rule; exclusive address ownership enforced; a daily billable-units fact traceable to lifecycle rows; retention billing decided and recorded; scale and rebuild cost reasoned; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: A volume is resized from 10 TB to 20 TB at 14:20. How is that day billed?
clarifications.a: By time-weighted size at the metering step: the minutes or hours at each size. State the partial-step rule.

clarifications.q: How do we know bytes stored in a bucket?
clarifications.a: From a daily inventory snapshot per bucket and class, and from change events in between. They can disagree; say which is authoritative.

clarifications.q: Is a detached volume billed?
clarifications.a: Yes, in this exercise. A volume is billed while it exists; attachment only matters for reporting and for deleting clusters safely.

clarifications.q: Can a bucket move between storage classes?
clarifications.a: Objects can, through lifecycle rules. A bucket can hold several classes at once, so the unit is bytes per class.

clarifications.q: What happens when a cluster is deleted?
clarifications.a: Its attachments end. Volumes and addresses stay with the customer until deleted or released, and keep billing.

hints: Model each resource as an entity plus an append-only history of state intervals (size, tier, class, owner, attachment); daily units are an integral over those intervals.
Keep attachments as their own intervals; never put a cluster_id column on the volume.
Define every unit in base units with the rounding step stated once, and derive daily facts from intervals clipped to the day.
followups: Compute one volume's GB-days for a day in which it was created at 09:00, resized at 14:20 and deleted at 22:00, under the {{metering_step}} rule. Show the rows that produce it.
A daily bucket inventory disagrees with the sum of change events by 3%. Which wins for billing, how is the difference corrected, and what does the customer see?
A public address is released and reassigned to another customer {{reassign_minutes}} minutes later. Show the intervals and each customer's address-hours for that day.
At {{resources}} resources with minute-level history, what do you keep at full grain, for how long, and what does the daily fact cost to rebuild for one corrected day?

rules.ask: A volume is detached from one cluster and attached to another at 11:00. With one column on the volume, which cluster held it at 10:59, and how do you report it?
A bucket grows from 1 TB to 100 TB at 23:00 and is emptied at 01:00. What does a once-a-day snapshot bill, and is that the rule you want?
Is retained-but-deleted storage billed in your model? Where is that decision recorded, and how does the customer see it?
Your daily GB-days are summed over a month across millions of resources. Where can rounding drift appear, and which base unit avoids it?
An address is released and reassigned within {{reassign_minutes}} minutes. What makes it impossible, in your model, for two customers to be charged for the same instant?

incidents: A volume resized twice in an hour was billed at the smaller size for the whole hour. With metering {{metering_step}}, the customer's daily export disagreed with the size history the console showed.
A release renamed a lifecycle state, and deleted volumes in their {{retention_days}}-day retention period were billed for some customers and not others for two weeks.

A public address was reassigned to a second customer {{reassign_minutes}} minutes after release, but the first customer's release event arrived late. Both customers were charged for the same address-hours.

templates.title: Delivered versus committed — GPUs ready against a contract's ramp, and shortfall GPU-days per month
templates.subtopic: calendar expansion, as-of joins over versioned schedules, interval snapshots, per-day floors

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud sells reserved capacity under contracts (this exercise's model; every contract, GPU type and number is hypothetical). A contract commits GPUs of one gpu_type from start_date through end_date (both inclusive), ramping up in steps. Contracts are amended: contract_amendments lists each contract's amendments with signed_on (amendment 0 is the original signing, on or before start_date), and every amendment restates the whole ramp in ramp_steps: from a step's effective_date, committed_gpus GPUs are committed until that amendment's next step. {{amend_note}} Nodes are provisioned into the customer's cluster against the contract; nodes records each node's GPU type, its GPU count, when it was requested, when it became ready (NULL if it never did) and when it was released (NULL if it is still running). Account teams want to see, for {{window_label}}, how delivery tracked each contract's ramp.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns contract_id, month, committed_gpu_days, ready_gpu_days, shortfall_gpu_days, short_days: one row per contract and calendar month that has at least one contract day between {{from_date}} and {{to_date}} (inclusive), ordered by contract_id, month. month is text in the form YYYY-MM.

  • The contract days are the dates from start_date through end_date that fall inside the window. Days are UTC calendar dates.
  • Committed on day d: the amendment in force on d is the contract's highest amendment_no with signed_on on or before d. The commitment is the committed_gpus of that amendment's step with the latest effective_date on or before d. Steps of any other amendment never apply on d.
  • Ready on day d (this exercise's rule: one measurement a day, at 00:00 UTC): the sum of gpus over the contract's nodes whose gpu_type is the contract's and that were ready at the start of d: ready_at at or before d 00:00, and released_at NULL or after d 00:00.
  • committed_gpu_days is the sum of the daily commitment over the month's contract days and ready_gpu_days the sum of the daily ready GPUs (more than committed counts in full). shortfall_gpu_days is the sum over those days of max(committed − ready, 0): a day with more GPUs ready never makes up for a short day. short_days is the number of days with ready below committed.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{contracts}} contracts, {{step_rows}} ramp-step rows and {{node_rows}} node rows; production has thousands of contracts, years of ramps and millions of node rows.
