sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, contracts, GPU types, regions and counts; check current docs for how any real contract measures delivery. requested_at and region are context and play no part in the calculation. Each amendment's ramp starts at the contract's start_date, so a commitment exists on every contract day.
sections.criteria: Contract days generated from the term and clipped to the window, not taken from node rows; the amendment in force chosen by signed_on per day and the latest step of that amendment only; the snapshot condition at 00:00 with the stated boundaries; nodes filtered by GPU type and summed by gpus; shortfall floored per day before aggregating; month formatted and ordered deterministically; can discuss an interval sweep for scale, minute-level delivery, as-known-on reporting and netting policy.

clarifications.q: A node became ready at 14:00 on the 3rd. Does it count on the 3rd?
clarifications.a: No. Each day is measured at 00:00 UTC, so it counts from the 4th. A node ready at exactly 00:00 on the 3rd counts on the 3rd.

clarifications.q: And a node released at exactly 00:00?
clarifications.a: It does not count that day: it must still be running after 00:00.

clarifications.q: An amendment signed on the 15th has a step effective on the 1st. Does it change the 1st to the 14th?
clarifications.a: No. Until the 15th the earlier amendment is in force. From the 15th, the new amendment's latest step on or before the day applies, which may be that back-dated step.

clarifications.q: Do nodes of another GPU type assigned to the contract count?
clarifications.a: No. Only nodes of the contract's gpu_type deliver against it.

clarifications.q: Should days after end_date appear, if nodes are still running?
clarifications.a: No. Only contract days count, and a month with no contract day in the window has no row.

hints: Expand each contract into its days with generate_series, clipped to both the term and the window.
For each contract day, find the amendment in force, then that amendment's latest step on or before the day (a correlated subquery with ORDER BY … LIMIT 1, or LATERAL).
LEFT JOIN the nodes on the snapshot condition, sum gpus with COALESCE per day, floor each day's shortfall at 0, and only then aggregate by month.
followups: In production this expands thousands of contracts into days and joins each day to millions of nodes. How would you compute ready GPUs per day without the day × node join?
The customer measures delivery by the minute, not at midnight. How would you compute GPU-minutes short, and which nodes change the answer most?
Finance wants this month's shortfall as it stood on the 1st, before an amendment signed on the 10th. What changes in the query, and what does the data model need to make that answer reproducible?
Over-delivery is not a credit against shortfall here. Make the case for and against netting within a week, and say who should decide.

rules.ask: One contract has three steps in each of two amendments. How many ramp rows does each day join to, and what does a SUM over that join give?
Is the contract's highest amendment in force on every day of the term, including days before it was signed?
Does every node carry the same number of GPUs? Which column says how many?
A node became ready at 14:00 on the 3rd. Which day does your condition count it on, and what does the rule say?
This runs once per contract-day. At production scale, how would you make the commitment lookup set-based?

incidents: An account review showed no shortfall for a month in which a customer had waited two weeks for nodes. An earlier version of this report netted over-delivered days against short ones.

An amendment signed mid-month back-dated a ramp step to the 1st. The report re-run after signing moved commitment into days before the amendment existed, and a conversation with the customer started from numbers that neither side had agreed for those days.

templates.title: Capacity that can be promised — sellable GPUs by region, type and month from installed, building and reserved supply
templates.subtopic: time-phased supply and demand, holds, uncertainty, as-of audit

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud sells capacity in {{regions}} regions and {{gpu_types}} GPU types, mostly through multi-year reservations whose contracts carry a ramp (so many GPUs from one month, more from a later month) and partly by the hour on demand. Supply comes from GPUs installed and accepted, from data halls under construction with an expected ready date and a power allocation, and from expansions still being planned. Demand comes from signed reservations, deals the sales teams are negotiating, a floor kept for on-demand customers, and spare held back for failures and maintenance. Account teams want to know, before they quote a delivery schedule, what can be promised in each region, GPU type and month over the next {{quarters}} quarters.
sections.problem: Design the capacity-promising system. Cover the inputs and who owns each one; the model of supply and demand per region, GPU type and month; how construction uncertainty is represented and what you promise against; tentative holds for deals in negotiation, with expiry, so that two account teams cannot promise the same GPUs; how a signed contract converts its hold into committed capacity; how a construction delay propagates to the contracts that depended on it and in what order shortfalls are assigned; the history that shows what was promisable on the day each contract was signed; and the interfaces for account teams, the contract system and operations.
sections.constraints: Committed capacity in any region, GPU type and month must never exceed the supply you chose to promise against, net of the on-demand floor and spare. A hold request is answered within a second, and concurrent holds must not both succeed for the same last GPUs. Every promise must be traceable to the supply snapshot and rules that allowed it. The data is small (thousands of rows a month), so the hard parts are correctness, concurrency, uncertainty and audit, not throughput.
sections.assumptions: All capacities, ramps, dates, spare fractions and power figures are hypothetical, and the rules are this exercise's (check current docs). GPU types do not substitute for each other unless a contract says so. Construction reports each hall's expected ready date as a range, and power for a hall is fixed by its power contract.
sections.criteria: Separates supply (installed, building with a date range, planned) from demand (commitments, holds, on-demand floor, spare); a time-phased ledger per region, GPU type and month built from appended events; promising against a stated conservative scenario, with the gap sold explicitly; holds as atomic all-months conditional writes with expiry; a documented, people-approved shortfall policy and dated options for affected contracts; as-of history that reproduces what was promisable on any date; interfaces that tell account teams why a hold failed; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is installed capacity certain?
clarifications.a: Installed and accepted GPUs are, apart from failures, which the spare covers. Halls under construction have a ready-date range; you decide which date you promise against.

clarifications.q: Can a deal be quoted for a region or GPU type with no free supply?
clarifications.a: Only as a waitlist or with a later start; the system must say which.

clarifications.q: How long does a hold last?
clarifications.a: This exercise's rule: 14 days, renewable once with approval; you decide what happens at expiry.

clarifications.q: Is the on-demand floor fixed?
clarifications.a: It is a business setting per region and GPU type, changed a few times a year; changes must not break existing commitments.

clarifications.q: Who decides which contract absorbs a shortfall?
clarifications.a: A documented policy you propose, applied by the system and approved by people; customers' names never decide it.

hints: Think of a time-phased ledger like available-to-promise in manufacturing: cells of (region, GPU type, month) with supply, the floor, spare, holds and commitments, each change an appended event.
Represent uncertain supply as dated scenarios (a likely date and a conservative date per hall) and promise only against the conservative one; sell the difference as a waitlist or with a stated risk.
A hold is a conditional write across every month of a ramp; it succeeds for all of them or for none.
followups: Walk through a hold for a ramp spanning seven months when one of those months has fewer free GPUs than the ramp needs. What does the account team see?
Two account teams place holds on the last GPUs of one region-month in the same second. What makes exactly one of them succeed?

A hall slips by {{slip_weeks}} weeks. Which contracts are affected, how is the shortfall assigned, and what options does the system offer (other region, other month, partial delivery, on-demand bridge)?
Finance asks whether promising against the likely date instead of the conservative one would have been worth the risk last year. What data answers that?
An auditor asks what was promisable in one region and GPU type on the day a particular contract was signed. Show how you answer exactly.

rules.ask: Airlines overbook knowing no-show rates. What is your equivalent of a no-show here, how would you measure it, and who carries the cost when it goes wrong?
Two account teams edit the spreadsheet at the same time for the same region. What stops both of them promising the same GPUs, and what is the audit trail?
Your forecast says a hall will be ready in March with 80% confidence. Which number goes into a signed contract, and why?
A seven-month ramp touches seven cells. What do you lock, in what order, and what happens to a hold that needs a month another hold is updating?
Which number in your design may be stale, and which must be exact at the moment a hold is granted?

incidents: A data hall that nine signed contracts are counting on for their ramps slips by {{slip_weeks}} weeks. Construction gives the new date as a range, and three more deals are waiting for holds against the same hall.

Two account teams place holds within the same second on the last 1,024 GPUs of one type in one region-month; both holds are confirmed, and the region-month is now promised beyond its conservative supply.
A problem found in acceptance testing withdraws 6% of one GPU type's installed GPUs in one region for three weeks, more than the spare held back for failures.

templates.title: Customer quota enforcement across regions — concurrent provisioning that never overshoots, and the increase workflow
templates.subtopic: quota claims, global caps split across regions, partitions, reconciliation

sections.scenario: {{customers}} customer organisations run GPU workloads in {{regions}} regions. Each organisation has quotas: the most GPUs of each type it may hold at once in each region, and for some organisations a global cap per GPU type across all regions. Nodes are requested through the API, the console, and the node-pool autoscaling of customers' Kubernetes clusters, so many requests from one organisation arrive concurrently in several regions; across the platform there are up to {{peak_requests}} provisioning requests a minute at peak. Customers who need more ask for an increase, which is reviewed against capacity within {{review_hours}} hours (this exercise's target).
sections.problem: Design quota enforcement. Cover the quota model (organisation, GPU type, region, optional global cap, effective dates); the admission check that claims quota before provisioning starts and releases it when provisioning fails or nodes are released; how usage is counted through the node lifecycle (requested, provisioning, ready, draining, released); how a global cap is enforced across regions that can be cut off from each other; reconciliation of quota counters with the nodes that actually exist; the increase workflow and its audit trail; and what customers see (limit, in use, pending, and why a request was refused).
sections.constraints: An organisation's GPUs in use plus in-flight claims never exceed its quota, under any interleaving of concurrent requests. Admission p99 under 300 ms. A region keeps admitting within its own quotas when it cannot reach the other regions. Quota is not capacity: a request within quota can still fail because the region has no free GPUs of that type, and the response must say which of the two refused it. Every quota change and increase decision is auditable.
sections.assumptions: Customer counts, request rates and review targets are hypothetical. Each region has its own provisioning control plane that emits node lifecycle events. Quotas and the increase process are this exercise's rules (check current docs).
sections.criteria: Quota modelled per organisation, GPU type and region with optional global caps and effective dates; admission as an atomic conditional claim with an idempotent claim id and expiry, released on failure; usage tied to explicit node lifecycle states; a global cap split into per-region allotments with rebalancing, conservative behaviour when partitioned, and a stated bound on any overshoot; reconciliation of counters with lifecycle events that only ever corrects in the safe direction first; quota refusals distinguished from capacity refusals; an auditable, partly automatic increase workflow; backpressure for retrying clients; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do nodes being drained still count?
clarifications.a: Yes, until they are released; the customer is still holding them.

clarifications.q: Is the global cap common?
clarifications.a: A minority of organisations have one, and they tend to be the largest.

clarifications.q: Can an increase be granted partly?
clarifications.a: Yes, for some regions, types or a smaller number, with a reason.

clarifications.q: Does a quota decrease evict running nodes?
clarifications.a: No. It blocks new requests until usage falls below the new limit.

clarifications.q: Who reviews increases?
clarifications.a: Capacity planners with an automatic first check; you design the check and what goes to a person.

hints: Make admission a claim: one conditional update that adds the requested GPUs to in_use + claimed only if the sum stays within the limit, with a claim id and an expiry.
A global cap across regions can be split into per-region allotments (escrow), so each region admits locally from its own share and rebalances when it can reach the others.
Counters drift. Recompute them from lifecycle events and the regions' own view of nodes, and decide which source wins.
followups: Two requests for 64 GPUs each arrive in the same millisecond when 100 remain in the organisation's quota. Walk through what each one sees.
Provisioning for a 64-GPU request gets 40 nodes ready and fails on the rest. What is counted against the quota now, and what does the customer see?
An organisation with a global cap scales in two regions while one of them is cut off from the global allotment service for 30 minutes. What does each region allow?

Reconciliation finds the counter for 200 organisations is higher than the nodes they hold. Which source do you trust, and how do you correct the counter without ever letting an organisation overshoot?
Increase requests spike before a holiday and capacity cannot cover them all. How does the workflow decide, and what keeps it fair and explainable?

rules.ask: The region holding the lock leader is cut off. Can the other regions still admit requests, and how much of the global cap can they use?
The cache holding quota counters restarts. What are the counters afterwards, and how do you know no organisation overshot while they were rebuilt?
A customer's cluster autoscaler retries every denied request immediately. What does that do to admission latency for everyone else in the region, and what do you return to slow it down?
Which count in your design may lag, and which must be exact when a claim is granted?
A request waits in your queue for quota to free up. How long, who sees it, and when is it refused instead?

incidents: After denials, one customer's cluster autoscaler sends 3,000 provisioning requests a minute for a single node pool, and admission p99 for every customer in that region rises from 120 ms to 2 seconds.

Release events for nodes freed during a two-hour control-plane outage in one of the {{regions}} regions were lost, so 40 organisations show as at quota while holding far fewer GPUs, and their clusters cannot scale.
An organisation with a global cap is admitted in two regions during a partition and holds 7% more GPUs of one type than its cap when the regions reconnect.

templates.title: Usage exports customers can reconcile — hourly files and an API that tie to the invoice to the cent
templates.subtopic: line-level usage, versioned restatements, rounding, tenant isolation

sections.scenario: {{customers}} customers buy GPU and CPU instances, storage and network transfer, some under reservations and some on demand. Their finance and cost teams want to reconcile each invoice to usage themselves: hourly usage files delivered to a storage bucket the customer owns or downloaded from the console, and an API over the same data, at line level — cluster, node or instance, GPU type, region, meter (GPU-seconds, CPU-seconds, storage byte-hours, transfer bytes), quantity, rate, whether the reservation or on-demand rate applied, and cost. The platform produces about {{lines_per_day}} usage lines a day. Metering data sometimes arrives late, and occasionally a metering error is found and corrected after the hour or the month has closed.
sections.problem: Design the usage export. Cover the line-level model with stable line ids; how an hour is closed and its file produced; how late data and corrections are published (new file versions, correction lines, or both) so that a customer who already loaded the old data can tell exactly what changed; how the invoice is computed from the same lines and where rounding happens so that the lines sum to the invoice exactly; the API (filters, pagination over a consistent snapshot); schema evolution; delivery into customer-owned buckets; tenant isolation; and the monitoring that proves the exports and invoices agree.
sections.constraints: For every invoice, the sum of the customer's exported lines for that period equals the invoice total exactly, in cents. The file for hour H is available within {{file_hours}} hours after H ends. Corrections found within {{restate_days}} days after month close restate that month; later ones appear as dated adjustments on the next invoice (this exercise's rule; check current docs). No floating point for money. One customer's usage must never appear in another customer's export, bucket or API response.
sections.assumptions: Customer counts, volumes and timings are hypothetical. Metering emits records per resource and meter with an event time and a record id; rates come from a versioned price book and each customer's contract terms (all hypothetical).
sections.criteria: Line-level model with deterministic ids and the rate basis on each line; hour closing with watermarks and a defined path for late records; versioned restatements with a manifest plus correction lines that work for both append and replace loaders; invoice computed from the same lines with one stated rounding step and a continuous tie-out check; consistent API snapshots; additive schema evolution with versions; tenant isolation by construction (per-customer paths derived from verified identity, write credentials scoped per customer, post-write verification); adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery, customer communication and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do customers load the files into their own warehouse?
clarifications.a: Many do, appending each hour; any restatement design must work for them.

clarifications.q: Can a line's cost be fractional cents?
clarifications.a: Rates can have more precision than cents. You decide where the one rounding to cents happens, and the lines must still sum to the invoice.

clarifications.q: Are credits (for example SLA credits) in the export?
clarifications.a: Yes, as their own lines, so the export explains the whole invoice.

clarifications.q: Format?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say how a new column is added without breaking a customer's loader.

clarifications.q: Can customers ask for a different granularity?
clarifications.a: Hourly is the base; daily and monthly are aggregations of the same lines.

hints: Give each line a deterministic id from (customer, resource, meter, hour, rate basis) so that a restated line replaces exactly the line it corrects.

Publish restatements as a new version of the affected hours with a manifest (which hours, which version, why), and also as signed correction lines, so append-only loaders and replace-by-hour loaders both converge.
Round once: either each line to cents with the invoice as their sum, or the invoice once with a visible rounding-adjustment line. State which, and test it at exact half cents.
followups: Walk through one hour: when is it closed, which late records still make it into the first file, and what happens to a record that arrives after?
A correction changes lines in 30 hours of last month for 300 customers. What exactly is published, and how does a customer who appends hourly files avoid double counting?
Where does rounding happen, and how do you prove the lines sum to the invoice for every customer every month?
A customer's bucket permissions change and deliveries start failing. How long do you retry, what do you tell them, and how do they catch up?
How would you show a customer, line by line, why this month's invoice differs from last month's?

rules.ask: Where exactly can a fraction of a cent exist in your pipeline, and where is it rounded?
A customer already loaded yesterday's version and appends new files. How do they learn that you replaced data, and what do they do?
You add a column for a new meter. What happens to a customer's loader written against last month's schema?
The export writer needs permission to write into thousands of customer-owned buckets. How do you keep one customer's data from ever landing in another's?
A restatement lands while a customer is paging through the API. Can they see a mix of old and new lines?

incidents: A metering fix found four days after month close changes 0.4% of lines for 300 customers whose invoices have already been sent, within the {{restate_days}}-day restatement window.
A customer reports that its hourly files for one month sum to $1,284.17 more than the invoice. It loaded both the original and the restated version of 20 hours.
A change to the export path template writes 14 hourly files for one customer under another customer's prefix for 40 minutes before it is caught.

templates.title: Network transfer metering — bytes per customer, region and destination class, billed without inspecting traffic contents
templates.subtopic: interface counters, destination classification, counter resets, data minimisation

sections.scenario: Customers' clusters, instances and storage in {{regions}} regions send and receive network traffic: to each other within a region, to other regions, to object storage, over private interconnects to the customer's own sites, and to the public internet. Transfer is billed by this exercise's rule (check current docs): inbound and same-region traffic are free; transfer between regions is billed at one rate; transfer to the internet is billed at another after the first {{free_gb}} GB a month per customer. The platform has about {{interfaces}} customer-attached virtual and physical interfaces, and the hosts and gateways that carry them report byte counters every {{report_seconds}} seconds.
sections.problem: Design network transfer metering. Cover where bytes are counted (host interfaces, gateways that handle public addresses and translation, interconnect ports) and how double counting between them is avoided; how each byte count is attributed to a customer and classified by destination class using address ranges that change over time; counter deltas, resets and wraparound; the aggregation pipeline to per-customer, per-region, per-class totals; the billable calculation including the free allowance; late and missing reports; what customers see; and the data you keep and for how long. Traffic contents are never inspected.
sections.constraints: No packet payload is captured, sampled or stored anywhere in the design. Billable bytes must come from counters, not from sampled flows. Address-range classifications apply from their effective time, and reclassifying history requires an explicit, audited restatement. Usage visible to customers within an hour; month totals final three days after month end. Per-connection records, if you keep any, are minimised and retained for a short, stated period.
sections.assumptions: Interface counts, reporting intervals, free allowances and rates are hypothetical. Each interface belongs to exactly one customer resource at a time, and the attachment history is available as events. Counters are 64-bit and reset when an agent or device restarts.
sections.criteria: Counters, not samples or contents, as the billing source, with one designated metering point per path and a rule against double counting; attribution through interface attachment history; destination classes from a bitemporal address-range table with audited restatements; reset, wraparound and out-of-order handling with plausibility bounds; per-customer aggregation with watermarks, late reports and exact month totals; the free allowance applied once per month at the right stage; data minimisation (no payloads, short retention of any per-connection data, customer-facing totals only); reconciliation against independent counters; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can we use sampled flow records for billing?
clarifications.a: You may use them for troubleshooting; billing must come from counters. Say why.

clarifications.q: How is the destination known without looking inside packets?
clarifications.a: From packet headers and routing: the destination address and the route or gateway the traffic leaves by, matched against a versioned table of address ranges and their class.

clarifications.q: Does a customer see per-connection detail?
clarifications.a: No. They see totals by region, destination class and resource; anything finer is for troubleshooting and is not billed.

clarifications.q: What if a host stops reporting?
clarifications.a: Its counters keep counting; the next report carries the bytes since the last one. You decide how the gap is spread across time.

clarifications.q: Do interconnect ports belong to one customer?
clarifications.a: Yes, dedicated ports do; shared gateways carry many customers and attribute bytes by the customer's address or network.

hints: Bill from per-interface (or per-customer-network) counters per destination class at the edge where the class is known; count each byte at exactly one designated metering point per path.

Compute deltas from monotonically increasing counters with an explicit reset rule (a lower value after a restart means the new value is the delta) and never trust a delta larger than the link could carry in the interval.
Keep the destination table bitemporal: what was true at the time of the traffic, and when we learned it.
followups: Trace one gigabyte from a customer's node to the internet through a gateway with a public address. Which device counts it, and which class does it get?
A host agent restarts and its counters start again from zero. Walk through the next report and what gets billed.
An address range moves from "internet" to "same region" because a storage endpoint moved. How do you apply that, and what about traffic already billed?
How do you show a customer that their bill is right without giving them, or keeping, per-connection data?
A region's metering pipeline is down for six hours. What do customers see, and how do month totals stay exact?

rules.ask: Sampling one packet in a thousand gives an estimate. Can a customer dispute an estimate on their invoice, and what do you show them?
What would you learn from contents that the headers and counters do not tell you, and why is it worth the risk of holding customers' traffic?
You keep per-connection records. Who can read them, for how long, and what do they reveal about a customer's own users?
A reported counter is lower than the last one. Is that a reset or a delayed, out-of-order report, and how do you tell?
A host's reports arrive out of order after a network blip. Does your stream compute negative deltas, and what does it bill?

incidents: A host agent upgrade restarts counters on 30,000 interfaces; the delta logic treats the lower readings as 64-bit wraparound and computes a charge of about 18 exabytes for several customers.

An address-range update is published with the wrong effective time, and for six hours traffic from one region to its own object storage is classified as internet transfer, which would overbill about 900 customers.

Traffic through gateways with public addresses is counted at both the host interface and the gateway for one region, so internet transfer for customers using public addresses is doubled for nine days before a customer notices that their usage exceeds their own measurements.

templates.title: Planned maintenance and regional status — scheduling across customers' windows, status pages and measured impact
templates.subtopic: maintenance scheduling, customer notice, status communication, impact measurement

sections.scenario: A GPU cloud in {{regions}} regions must regularly patch firmware, drivers and operating systems, replace hardware, and do electrical and cooling work that takes whole rows of a data hall offline. {{customers}} customers declare maintenance preferences: weekly allowed windows in their own time zone, at most {{max_share}}% of their nodes in one cluster under maintenance at once, and occasional freeze periods (for example around a launch). Planned work announced at least {{notice_days}} days ahead and done inside the announced window does not count against the availability SLA (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Each region also has a public status page showing the state of each service.
sections.problem: Design the maintenance and status system. Cover the inputs (work items with the nodes, racks or rows they touch, durations and dependencies; customers' windows, limits and freezes); how a schedule is computed and conflicts are surfaced to people; notices and how changes to a planned event are communicated; execution through customers' Kubernetes clusters (cordoning and draining nodes, described generally) with abort criteria; regional status pages and who or what may change them; and how customer impact is measured (node-minutes unavailable per customer, inside or outside the announced window) so that SLA exclusions are applied only where the rule allows.
sections.constraints: No customer cluster ever has more than {{max_share}}% of its nodes under planned maintenance at once. Work that cannot fit a customer's windows within 30 days is raised to people, not silently scheduled. Windows are honoured in the customer's local time across daylight-saving changes. The status page never shows "operational" for a service that is failing for many customers, and never shows a regional outage because of one monitoring signal. Impact measurements are reproducible from recorded events.
sections.assumptions: Region and customer counts, notice periods and limits are hypothetical. Node lifecycle events (cordoned, drained, in maintenance, returned) are recorded with times. Customers can acknowledge a notice or ask to move it; the platform may decline when the work is urgent.
sections.criteria: Work items, customer windows, limits and freezes modelled explicitly with local-time rules; a scheduler that enforces the per-cluster limit across all concurrent work items and surfaces conflicts to people; notices with versioned changes and acknowledgements; execution through cordon and drain with timeouts, abort criteria and handling of blocked drains; status derived from several customer-facing signals with human confirmation for major states and automatic publication limited to clear cases; impact measured from lifecycle events against announced windows, with SLA exclusions applied only where the rule allows and reproducible per customer; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery, communication and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is emergency work (a security fix) different?
clarifications.a: Yes. It may need shorter notice; it then does not qualify for the SLA exclusion under this exercise's rule, and the design should make that visible.

clarifications.q: Can a whole row's power work be split?
clarifications.a: No; it takes all nodes in those racks at once. Customers with many nodes there are the hard case.

clarifications.q: What if a drain is blocked by the customer's own disruption limits in their cluster?
clarifications.a: The work waits up to a stated time, then either proceeds with notice or is rescheduled; you choose and justify.

clarifications.q: Who owns the status page?
clarifications.a: Operations; automation may propose changes, and you decide which it may publish on its own.

clarifications.q: Do customers see each other's maintenance?
clarifications.a: No. A customer sees its own events; the status page shows only regional and service-level state.

hints: Store windows as recurring local-time rules with an IANA time zone, and expand them into UTC intervals only for the dates you schedule.

Treat each work item as a set of nodes and each customer's limit as a capacity per cluster per time slot; the schedule is a constrained assignment that people review, not a single greedy pass hidden from them.
Measure impact from node lifecycle events joined to the announced events, so "inside the window" is computed, not reported.
followups: Walk through scheduling power work for one row that holds nodes from 40 customers with different windows and limits.
The work overruns its window by three hours. What happens automatically, what do customers hear, and how is the SLA exclusion applied?
How does the status page decide between "operational", "degraded", "planned maintenance" and "outage" for a service in a region, and who approves each change?
A daylight-saving change is coming next week. What in your design could drain nodes an hour outside a customer's window, and how do you test it?
Over a quarter, how do you show each customer how much of its unavailability was planned and inside windows, and how do you use the same data to reduce maintenance impact?

rules.ask: A customer's disruption limits block the drain indefinitely. Does your maintenance wait, override, or reschedule, and who decides?
Your scheduler finds no plan that fits every customer's window this month. What does it produce, and who sees the conflict?
A customer's window is 02:00–04:00 local on the night clocks go back. Which two hours do you use, and does the customer agree?
One synthetic check fails in a region at 03:00. What does the status page show, and who is woken?
The work started inside the window and finished outside it. Which node-minutes are excluded, and how would a customer verify that?

incidents: Power work in one hall overruns its window by three hours, and nodes of 120 customers stay out of service past the time announced {{notice_days}} days earlier.
Windows were stored as fixed UTC offsets, so after a daylight-saving change 60 customers have nodes drained an hour outside their allowed window.
A drain wave for a driver update takes 30% of one customer's cluster at once, above its {{max_share}}% limit, because two work items scheduled independently overlapped on the same cluster.
The status page shows "operational" for 50 minutes while node provisioning fails in one region, because the page is derived only from the health of running nodes.

templates.title: Telling a customer that capacity they planned around will arrive late
templates.subtopic: evidence, options, commitments, working with account teams

customer_plan: a large training run starting on the ramp date
an inference expansion ahead of their own seasonal peak
a product launch promised to their own customers

sections.scenario: You lead the team that owns the delivery forecast for reserved capacity: the data that says when GPUs in each region will be ready for each contract's ramp. Your team's latest numbers show that {{share}} of the next ramp step for one customer will be ready about {{delay_weeks}} weeks late, because a data hall is behind schedule. The customer has planned {{customer_plan}} around that date. The account team owns the relationship and has not been told yet; the next scheduled call with the customer is in five days.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you make sure the delay and its range are real before anyone is told; who should tell the customer, when, and with what; the options you prepare (another region, another GPU type, a partial delivery, a temporary bridge with on-demand capacity, a changed ramp) and how you check each one is actually available; what you commit to and what you refuse to commit to; and how you keep the customer and the account team updated until the capacity is delivered. Then tell me about a real time you had to deliver bad news about a date to someone who depended on it, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You are not the account owner and do not negotiate contract terms; any remedy under the contract is the account and legal teams' decision, and every term here is hypothetical. The construction date itself is uncertain: the hall team gives a range, not a date. Other customers may be counting on the same hall.
sections.assumptions: The customer, figures and dates are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Verifies the delay and its range with the owning team before acting and states uncertainty honestly; insists on an early warning through the account owner rather than waiting for certainty, and prepares the account team with facts, a range and a date for the next update; prepares concrete options and checks they exist before offering them; commits to dates only at a stated confidence and to updates on a schedule; treats affected customers consistently under a documented rule; respects decision rights on contract remedies; follows through until delivery and changes the forecasting so later slips are seen earlier; real example with what they personally did and how it landed, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How sure is the forecast?
clarifications.a: The hall team gives a range: the delay could be shorter or longer by about two weeks.

clarifications.q: Is there spare capacity elsewhere?
clarifications.a: Some, in another region and partly in a different GPU type; whether it fits the customer's workload is unknown.

clarifications.q: Does sales want to wait until the date is certain?
clarifications.a: The account lead would prefer to wait a week "until we know more".

clarifications.q: Are other customers affected?
clarifications.a: Two smaller customers have ramp steps against the same hall.

hints: Separate what is known, what is estimated (with a range), and what is not known yet; say each plainly.
Bad news gets worse with time; give the customer the earliest honest warning with a date for the next update.
Options are only options if someone has checked they exist; reserve them tentatively before offering them.
followups: The account lead wants to wait a week. What do you say, and what evidence do you bring?
Which options would you prepare, and how would you check that each one would actually work for the customer's workload?
The customer asks you to promise the new date in writing. What do you say?
The two smaller customers are affected too. Do they hear at the same time, and who decides how the capacity that does arrive is shared?
In your real example, what did you say first, and what did the other person do with the news?

rules.ask: The customer finds out from someone else in the meantime. What does that do to every later date you give them?
The range is plus or minus two weeks. Which date do you commit to, and what happens if you miss that one too?
What exactly do you bring to the executive, and what decision do you need from them?
You do not own contract terms. How do you make sure the customer is not promised something before the right people decide?
What did you personally say or do, and when?

templates.title: Processes that worked for a small company breaking during very fast growth
templates.subtopic: diagnosing what breaks, proportionate process, change without paralysis

growth: engineering headcount tripled in a year
the number of customers grew tenfold in eighteen months
the platform went from two regions to nine in two years
process: capacity tracked in a shared spreadsheet that several teams edit
every production schema change reviewed by one senior engineer
an on-call rota shared by everyone who can deploy
billing questions answered by whoever wrote the query last

sections.scenario: The company has grown fast: {{growth}}. Many of the ways of working that served it well when it was small are still in place, among them {{process}}. In the last quarter there were {{incidents}} incidents or near misses that trace back, at least in part, to that way of working. People who built it are proud of it, and some say the answer is simply to be more careful.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you establish what is actually failing and why (rather than who); how you decide what to replace, what to keep and what to change only a little; how you design the replacement so that it fits the size of the problem and does not slow everything down; how you get the people who run the current way of working to own the change; how you roll it out without stopping the business; and how you will know it worked. Then tell me about a real time you changed a way of working that had stopped scaling, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You lead one team; the way of working spans several teams. Growth will not slow down while you fix it. The people involved are respected and stretched.
sections.assumptions: The company, figures and incidents are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses from the incidents rather than from opinion, finding the structural cause (a single person, a manual step, no source of truth) without blaming individuals; proposes a proportionate replacement that removes the failure mode rather than adding gates, sized to the growth rate; brings the people who run the current way of working into the design and the ownership; rolls out incrementally with a measurable outcome and a review date; acknowledges what the old way did well and keeps it; real example with personal contribution, resistance and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is leadership asking for a fix?
clarifications.a: Your director agrees there is a problem and wants a proposal, not a big programme.

clarifications.q: Did the incidents hurt customers?
clarifications.a: One of them did, briefly; the rest were caught in time.

clarifications.q: Is there a budget for tools?
clarifications.a: Small; time from your team is the main resource.

clarifications.q: Have earlier fixes been tried?
clarifications.a: A checklist was added last year; it is filled in inconsistently.

hints: Look at the incidents together: what do they have in common, and which part of the way of working failed in each?
A good replacement removes a single point of failure or a manual step; a bad one adds approvals.
Change the smallest thing that would have prevented most of the incidents, then measure.
followups: How would you analyse the {{incidents}} incidents to find what the way of working actually got wrong?
Someone says the answer is to be more careful. How do you respond without dismissing them?
Describe the replacement you would propose for {{process}}. What does it cost, and who has to do something differently?
Six months later, how do you know the change worked and did not just move the risk somewhere else?
In your real example, what resistance did you meet, and what changed your mind about part of your own proposal?

rules.ask: The tool takes a quarter to build. What do you change next week so the next incident is less likely?
How long will a change wait for your new approval step at today's growth rate, and what will people do to get around it?
The people involved were already careful. What about the way of working let a careful person make the mistake?
Who owns the new way of working a year from now, and how do they know it is still working?
What did you personally do or decide?

templates.title: A customer's security review your platform cannot yet fully satisfy
templates.subtopic: honest answers, compensating controls, roadmap commitments

gap: customer-managed encryption keys for one storage service
per-customer logs of every operator access to their resources
evidence that one shared networking component isolates tenants
certified deletion of a customer's data within a stated number of days after they leave
pressure: an account executive has already replied 'yes' to that question in an email
the deal would be the largest in the region this year
a competitor has told the prospect it supports this today

sections.scenario: A prospective customer sends a security questionnaire before signing a reservation. Your team owns the platform area it asks about, and one requirement is {{gap}}. Today the platform supports it only in part. The prospect wants answers in {{weeks}} weeks, and {{pressure}}.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you establish exactly what the platform does today, with evidence; how you write an answer that is accurate and useful rather than a bare no; which compensating controls or interim arrangements you could offer, and how you make sure they are real; whether and how you commit to closing the gap, and who has to agree before anything is promised; how you handle the pressure that comes with the deal (here, {{pressure}}); and what you do after the answer is sent. Then tell me about a real time you had to give an honest answer that put a deal, a launch or a relationship at risk, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Security and legal teams own the final wording of any security answer; you own the technical facts. A wrong answer in a questionnaire can become a contractual commitment. Roadmap items need the owning teams' agreement and capacity.
sections.assumptions: The prospect, requirement and dates are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Establishes the facts with evidence and corrects documentation that overstates them; asks why the requirement matters to the prospect and answers the underlying risk; writes an accurate answer that states what exists, what does not and what mitigates the gap, through the security and legal owners; corrects an inaccurate earlier answer promptly, starting privately with the colleague and the account lead; offers only compensating controls that are real and verifiable; makes roadmap commitments only with the owning teams' agreement and frames the trade-off for the decider; follows through after the answer; real example with what honesty cost and earned, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the partial support documented?
clarifications.a: Partly; the documentation is a year old and you suspect it overstates one detail.

clarifications.q: Could the gap be closed?
clarifications.a: Your team estimates about a quarter of work, which would displace something already planned.

clarifications.q: Does the prospect need it on day one?
clarifications.a: Unknown; the questionnaire does not say why they ask.

clarifications.q: Who talks to the prospect?
clarifications.a: The account team, with you on a call if useful.

hints: Start by finding out why the prospect asks: the risk they want covered may be met another way.
Describe precisely what exists, what does not, and what would mitigate the gap, in words a security reviewer can test.
A roadmap date given to win a deal is a commitment; get it agreed by those who will do the work, or do not give it.
followups: How do you find out what the platform really does today, and what do you do about the documentation that may overstate it?
Suppose an account executive had already replied 'yes' to the question in an email. How do you correct it, and with whom first?
The prospect accepts an interim control plus a date. What has to be true inside your organisation before that date is sent?
Your director asks whether the quarter of work should displace the planned item. How do you frame that decision?
In your real example, what did honesty cost, and what did it earn?

rules.ask: A reviewer later finds that the answer was technically true but misleading. What happens to the relationship and to your company's other answers?
Who agreed to that date, and what moves out of the plan to make room for it?
How would the prospect's security team verify that your interim control works?
What decision do you need from them, and what options do you put in front of them?
What did you personally write or say?

templates.title: Running a pre-mortem before a high-stakes launch
templates.subtopic: pre-mortems, turning risks into owned actions, go/no-go criteria

launch: a new region opening to customers
a new billing system taking over from the old one at the start of a month
self-service on-demand clusters opening to all customers at once
per-second metering replacing hourly metering on every invoice

sections.scenario: In {{weeks}} weeks the company launches {{launch}}. The work spans {{teams}} teams, the date has been announced to customers, and everyone says things are on track. You are the technical lead accountable for the launch going well, and you want to run a pre-mortem: imagine it is a month after launch and it has gone badly, and work out why.
sections.problem: How do you run it? Cover who you invite and how you make it safe for people to name risks in other teams' work and in senior people's plans; how you structure the session so it produces specific failure stories rather than generic worries; how you sort and size what comes out; how each important risk becomes an action with an owner and a date, a test, a monitor or a rollback plan; the go/no-go criteria you set for launch day and who decides; and how you follow up so the pre-mortem is not forgotten. Then tell me about a real time you ran or took part in a risk review before a launch, what it caught or missed, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The date does not move without a director's decision. Teams are busy, and a session that produces a long list with no owners will be ignored. Some of the risks will be in work owned by people more senior than you.
sections.assumptions: The launch, teams and timings are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Invites the people who know the failure modes across all teams, including operations and support, and makes it safe to raise risks (silent writing first, the facilitator naming that risks in senior people's work are expected); produces specific failure stories, sorts them by likelihood and cost, and focuses on cross-team and unowned risks; turns the important ones into owned, dated actions favouring detection, rehearsed rollback and limited blast radius (for example a staged opening); sets measurable go/no-go criteria with a named decider; follows up on open risks and escalates with evidence when needed; real example with what was caught and missed, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has anything like this launched before here?
clarifications.a: Not at this scale; there is no previous launch to copy.

clarifications.q: Can you delay the launch?
clarifications.a: Only by asking the director with evidence.

clarifications.q: Is there a rollback?
clarifications.a: Each team has said it has one; nobody has tested them together.

clarifications.q: How long can the session be?
clarifications.a: Ninety minutes, with follow-ups afterwards.

hints: Ask each person to write their failure stories alone before anyone speaks, so the first or most senior voice does not set the agenda.
Size each risk by likelihood and by the cost if it happens, and look hardest at the ones nobody owns or that cross team boundaries.
Prefer actions that make a failure detectable and reversible over actions that try to make it impossible.
followups: What three failure stories would you expect to come up for {{launch}}, and which would worry you most?
A senior engineer dismisses a risk raised about their team's work. How do you handle it in the room and afterwards?
Which go/no-go criteria would you set, and what evidence would each need on launch day?
Two weeks before launch, a risk from the pre-mortem is still open and its owner says there is no time. What do you do?
In your real example, what did the review catch, and what did it miss?

rules.ask: The most senior person speaks first and names two risks. How many people now raise something different?
The list has 60 items. Which ten get owners this week, and how did you choose them?
Has the rollback been run end to end across all {{teams}} teams? What would you learn by trying it?
What evidence would you put in front of the director, and what would you need to see to recommend launching on time instead?
What did you personally do in the session and after it?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a GPU cloud sold by reservation and by the hour
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, metering to the cent, as-of capacity and tenant isolation

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: usage metered per second and invoiced to the cent, reconcilable by each customer
committed capacity answerable as of any past date, through every contract amendment
each customer seeing only its own usage, clusters and status
network usage metered from counters without inspecting traffic contents
scale: hundreds of thousands of GPUs across many regions
billions of metered usage records a day

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for a GPU cloud sold by reservation and by the hour, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The GPU cloud setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example integer base units and exact rates with one stated rounding step and line-level exports that sum to the invoice; a bitemporal record of contracts, ramps and amendments; tenant scoping derived from verified identity in every query path and export; byte counters with reset handling and destination classes from a versioned address table, with no payload capture); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a cloud or billing system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, start from one GPU-hour: where it is measured, which ids and timestamps it carries, and which of them the new requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
Where in your system could a fraction of a cent appear, and where exactly is it rounded?
A metering fix changes last month's usage after invoices went out. Which numbers change, and what does a customer see changing?
How do you make sure one customer can never see another customer's usage in that, even through a misconfigured path or filter?
